sections.h2: What are the choices for selling a house in Quincy, Illinois?
sections.html:
A Quincy homeowner can list with an agent, sell privately, or accept a direct offer from a buyer who pays cash and buys the house in its current condition. The best fit depends on the age of the house, how much work it needs, and how long you can wait.

Quincy has several historic districts, and many of its brick homes date to the German immigrant building boom of the late 1800s. Those houses charm some buyers and put off others who dread the cost of updating them. Think through which of these describes your situation:

  • The house is in good shape and you have months to wait for the right buyer, so a listing makes sense.
  • The house needs a roof, furnace or foundation work that you would rather not pay for.
  • You inherited it from a parent who lived there for decades and want to settle the estate.
  • A tenant, a code complaint or a lien is complicating a conventional sale.

For the last three situations, a direct sale can save time, because there is no lender appraisal to pass. Whatever route you choose, get the price, closing date and who pays which costs in writing first.

sections.h2: What does the Census say about Quincy housing?
sections.html:
Quincy is a lower-priced market with a sizable rental share. Only 63.6 percent of occupied homes are owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024, so investors and landlords are active buyers here as well as families.

The city has lost a little population since 2010, when the census counted 40,633 residents. The population peaked decades ago, and about one in five residents is 65 or older. Many of the people selling are long-time owners downsizing or heirs handling a parent's house. A mean commute of about 14 minutes is a point worth mentioning to buyers.

sections.h2: How do the bluffs, river and neighborhoods shape a Quincy sale?
sections.html:
Quincy sits on bluffs above the Mississippi River at Quincy Bay, with a floodplain across the river in Missouri and the Quincy Hills to the east. Houses on sloping lots near the river deserve a close look at drainage, retaining walls and basement moisture before you list.

The city is compact, at about 15.8 square miles, and buyers tend to think in terms of areas. Downtown is a historic district, and the South Side German Historic District holds the brick homes built by German immigrants in the late 1800s, including the Dick Brothers Brewery buildings from 1857. North Quincy lies beyond a rail line and a large creek, and Hickory Grove sits to the east along Interstate 172.

  • Illinois Route 104 (Broadway) runs from the river bridges east to Interstate 172.
  • Illinois Route 96 doubles as the Great River Road, and Illinois Route 57 links U.S. 24 downtown to Interstate 172.
  • U.S. Route 24 crosses the river on the Quincy Memorial Bridge and the Bayview Bridge.
  • Interstate 72 passes about 12 miles south of town.

If your house is in or near a historic district, mention its architecture in any description. Original woodwork, stained glass and brick details are things buyers in these areas look for.

sections.h2: What drives Quincy's economy and demand for homes?
sections.html:
Quincy's largest employers anchor steady demand for housing. Blessing Hospital, Quincy Public Schools and Titan International are listed as the top three employers in the area, and Niemann Foods, Gardner Denver, Kohl Wholesale and Knapheide Manufacturing are among the companies based in town.

Higher education adds renters and buyers as well. Quincy University, John Wood Community College, Gem City College and the Blessing-Rieman College of Nursing and Health Sciences are all in or near the city, and the public school district is Quincy Public School District 172. Employers and campuses of that size keep a base of local buyers and renters in the market.

Census figures put health care and social assistance receipts in Quincy at about $1.3 billion for 2022. The Quincy and Hannibal area forms a combined statistical area of roughly 116,000 people, so some buyers come from across the river in Missouri.

sections.h2: What city rules should a Quincy seller check?
sections.html:
Quincy's Office of Inspection, on the second floor of City Hall at 730 Maine Street, handles building permits and minimum housing complaints. The city runs a complaint-driven system for rentals, where a tenant files a Minimum Housing Complaint Form and an inspector visits. If you are selling a rental, ask the Office of Inspection whether any registration or inspection requirement applies to your address.

The housing complaint form lists the items inspectors check against the International Property Maintenance Code. Working smoke detectors in each bedroom and hallway, carbon monoxide alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage, handrails on stairs with more than four risers, a watertight roof and a heating system that holds 68 degrees are among them. A buyer's inspector will look at the same items, so fix them early.

The city has also had a Small Rental Rehabilitation Program for owners of small rental buildings west of 18th Street, but the program page states that the city is not currently offering it. Do not count on that money when pricing a repair-heavy house.

sections.h2: How does a Quincy sale get recorded in Adams County?
sections.html:
Adams County records deeds at the Recorder of Deeds office at 507 Vermont Street in Quincy. The recorder's page says every deed or trust document must come with an Illinois Department of Revenue Real Estate Transfer Declaration or a Statement of Exemption.

The county's fee table lists a minimum of $80.00 for land records under 50 pages on standard paper, $92.00 for documents that do not meet the standards in 55 ILCS 5/3-5018, and $80.00 for each additional book and page reference. Those figures reflect the added Rental Housing Support Fee that took effect July 1, 2023. Fees change, so confirm with the office before closing.

Illinois also requires the seller to give the buyer a completed residential disclosure report before the contract is signed (765 ILCS 77/20). Under the next section, a seller is not required to investigate, but must disclose material defects the seller actually knows about. Keep records of any work done on the house.

faqs.q: Is it hard to sell an older brick house in Quincy?
faqs.a: It can take longer, since buyers want proof that wiring, plumbing and the foundation are sound. A listing may reach buyers who value historic details, while a direct sale suits an owner who wants to skip repairs.

faqs.q: What does Adams County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: The county's posted minimum for land records is $80.00 for documents under 50 pages that meet the paper standards, and $92.00 for documents that do not. Confirm the current schedule with the Recorder of Deeds before closing.

faqs.q: Does Quincy require a rental registration for landlords selling a house?
faqs.a: The city's housing complaint process is tenant-driven, and an inspector visits after a complaint. Ask the Office of Inspection at City Hall whether any registration applies to your property before you list a rental.

faqs.q: Who inspects Quincy houses for code problems?
faqs.a: The city's Office of Inspection, at 730 Maine Street, reviews minimum housing complaints and building permits. A tenant files the complaint form and an inspector schedules a visit.

faqs.q: How many people live in Quincy?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau estimated 38,918 residents on July 1, 2025, down from 39,463 at the 2020 census. Quincy is the Adams County seat on the Mississippi River.
